top_choice_rationale: P001 (Kiyotaki and Moore, B040) has the clearest attribution on the slate: the originating 1997 paper has two authors and no co-originator is left out. It isolates one general mechanism, in which collateral-limited borrowing feeds back on asset prices and makes shocks larger and more persistent. After nearly three decades of extension, critique and use in macro-finance and policy modelling, the achievement is mature. The citation should credit the mechanism and its influence on how credit cycles and crises are modelled, not a settled amplification magnitude. Reservations remain: direct empirical validation is indirect, the overlap with the 2022 prize is unverified, and leaving out Gertler and Gilchrist favours theory over tested evidence. I rank P002 (Autor, Dorn and Hanson, narrowed to the trade-shock evidence) a close second. It is credibly identified and cleanly attributed as a three-author design, but its record is about a decade shorter. P003 (Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn) is a mature methodological contribution whose credibility depends on functional-form and instrument assumptions. Any of the three awards is preferable to no award, so P000 is last.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile: no co-authorship or institutional tie to Kiyotaki, Moore, Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Pakes, Berry or Levinsohn. My market-design field lies outside all three proposals. I am an SSE affiliate alongside committee colleagues Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Strömberg, which is a tie to colleagues and not to candidates. I gave the 2020 presentation speech, which reflected the Academy and does not establish a preference here.
